rows.theme: A polling card that tells one voter where to vote, when, and what to bring.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: One sheet, three facts and a deadline: small enough to finish properly, large enough that every hierarchy decision is visible.
pitfalls: Becomes a leaflet explaining how voting works rather than a card about this person's station
The station address loses the top of the page to a crest and a council logo
Students invent the ID rules; the task is presenting rules, not writing them
rows.too_big_variant: An electoral services site covering registration, postal votes and results.

rows.theme: A response form for a local planning notice, for someone who has never read one.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: The content is genuinely hard and genuinely public, so every layout choice has to be argued rather than styled.
pitfalls: Turns into a petition — a form offering only 'object' has stopped being a consultation
Free-text boxes with no prompt return blank; writing the prompt is the design work
Legal wording is pasted in whole instead of paired with a plain summary
rows.too_big_variant: The council's whole planning portal, with maps, case histories and officer reports.

rows.theme: A jury summons letter a person can act on without ringing to ask what it means.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: One high-stakes document where tone, hierarchy and the reply deadline compete openly, which is what a beginner needs to see.
pitfalls: The date you must reply by ends up smaller than the crest above it
Threatening tone is treated as fixed rather than as something the designer chose
The envelope gets redesigned and the letter inside never does
rows.too_big_variant: Every letter a courts service sends, redesigned as one correspondence system.

rows.theme: A council tax bill showing what was charged, why, and what to do if it is wrong.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: Numbers a student did not choose, in a hierarchy they must choose, with a dispute route that is usually buried.
pitfalls: The total is set large and the payment date is not
The breakdown table is styled before it is decided what the reader is comparing
'How to query this' is left as a phone number in the footer
rows.too_big_variant: A billing account area covering direct debits, arrears and every year's history.

rows.theme: A set of signs taking a pedestrian from one station exit to three civic buildings.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: Position, scale and reading distance stop being abstract the moment the reader is walking past at speed.
pitfalls: Designed at desk distance and never checked at four metres
All three destinations given equal weight, so the sign decides nothing
Arrows added last, as decoration, rather than as the grammar of the set
rows.too_big_variant: A wayfinding system for the whole city centre.

rows.theme: Reporting a noise problem to a council, from first screen to a reference number.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: A short flow with a real emotional temperature, and an ending — the reference number — that most student flows forget to design.
pitfalls: The confirmation screen says 'thank you' and not what happens next or when
Asks for the address before asking what the problem is
Becomes a complaints dashboard for council staff instead of the resident's flow
rows.too_big_variant: A whole environmental health case management system.

rows.theme: Finding out which bin goes out this week at one address.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: A single question with a single answer, so the portfolio has to be about clarity rather than about features.
pitfalls: The answer arrives as a twelve-month calendar instead of 'the green one, tomorrow'
Colour alone carries which bin, which fails the moment it is printed
A postcode field with no memory, so the same address is typed every week
rows.too_big_variant: A waste services site with bulky collections, recycling guides and permits.

rows.theme: Checking your position on a council allotment waiting list, and what it means.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: A number with no action attached to it — the design problem is making a long wait feel handled rather than ignored.
pitfalls: Shows a position and no sense of movement, which reads as a dead page
An estimated date is invented to fill the space, which the council could not honour
Turns into a plot-booking system nobody on the list can use yet

rows.theme: Ordering one repeat prescription and knowing when it can be collected.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: Small, repeated, and consequential: the same task done monthly exposes every friction a one-off flow hides.
pitfalls: Medicine names are set in one weight, so the reader cannot tell dose from brand
'Ordered' and 'ready to collect' are shown as the same state
Students design for a first-time user of a task people do forty times
rows.too_big_variant: A full patient record area with results, referrals and appointments.

rows.theme: An appointment letter that survives being stuck to a fridge for three weeks.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: The artefact has a known life — pinned up, glanced at, carried in — and that life should drive the layout.
pitfalls: Date, time and place are separated by two paragraphs of preamble
What to bring is written as prose rather than as a list you can check against
The cancellation number is set in the same size as the hospital's address
rows.too_big_variant: An appointments system covering booking, rescheduling and reminders.

rows.theme: The dispensing label on a box of tablets, for a reader holding three other boxes.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: A severe space constraint with a real cost of error, which forces genuine decisions about what is dropped.
pitfalls: The patient's name is given more room than the dose
Warnings are stacked so uniformly that none of them reads as a warning
Designed as one label, never as three sitting side by side on a table

rows.theme: Checking in for a clinic appointment at a kiosk in a busy waiting room.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: Standing, watched by a queue, one finger, no help nearby — constraints a student can feel without any research budget.
pitfalls: Date of birth entry designed for a mouse and a keyboard
Confirmation flashes and clears before the person has looked up
Text height set for a phone in the hand, not a screen at arm's length
rows.too_big_variant: A patient administration system covering arrivals, triage and room allocation.

rows.theme: Keeping a two-week symptom diary to take to one appointment.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: Entry is daily and dull; the payoff is a single summary — a clean argument about designing for the boring middle.
pitfalls: Entry takes two minutes a day, so it is abandoned on day four
A ten-point severity scale nobody can use consistently
The summary the clinician actually reads is never designed at all
rows.too_big_variant: A general health tracker covering sleep, mood, exercise and medication.

rows.theme: Getting a visitor from a hospital main entrance to one named outpatient clinic.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: Decision points are countable and the failure is obvious: the visitor stops walking and looks around.
pitfalls: Signs name departments the visitor's letter does not name
Every junction repeats all destinations instead of pruning to what is ahead
Colour-coded routes with no second cue, unusable for a colour-blind visitor
rows.too_big_variant: Signage for the entire hospital estate including car parks and wards.

rows.theme: Reading your own blood test results before anyone has explained them.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: Forces the hardest Level 4 question — what does a reader need withheld, and who decided — with no visual trickery available.
pitfalls: Out-of-range values styled in red, which reads as danger rather than as 'discuss this'
Reference ranges shown without saying what a range is
Students write the clinical interpretation themselves, which is not theirs to write
rows.too_big_variant: A complete patient portal with records, letters and messaging.

rows.theme: A one-page instruction sheet for using an inhaler correctly, for a new user.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: Sequence, illustration and text have to cooperate on one page, and the order of steps cannot be argued with.
pitfalls: Steps illustrated beautifully and numbered ambiguously
The most-failed step is given the same weight as the easiest one
Becomes a poster about asthma rather than instructions for one device

rows.theme: Taking out cash at a machine in the street, at night, with someone waiting behind.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: A short flow where timing, privacy and physical context matter more than aesthetics — rare and useful at this level.
pitfalls: The card and the cash are returned in an order the design never decided
Balance shown on screen by default, in public
Amount options set for the designer's own habits rather than a range of users
rows.too_big_variant: A whole banking self-service estate including paying in and statements.

rows.theme: A payslip that shows what was earned, what was taken, and what to query.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: Dense tabular content that a student cannot invent, so all the work goes into grouping, alignment and emphasis.
pitfalls: Every deduction is given equal weight, so nothing can be scanned
Year-to-date and this-month columns are not visually distinguished
Abbreviations are carried over unexplained because they were in the source
rows.too_big_variant: A payroll self-service portal with P60s, expenses and pension statements.

rows.theme: The letter telling someone their account has gone into an unarranged overdraft.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: Bad news with a required action and a legal minimum: the student must design tone, not just type.
pitfalls: Softened until the reader does not realise they are being charged
The fee is stated and the way to stop it accruing is not
Students rewrite the regulated wording rather than working around it

rows.theme: A till receipt a person can use to return one item three weeks later.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: An everyday object nobody has looked at closely, and a clear second purpose that its layout usually ignores.
pitfalls: Designed for the shop's records rather than the customer's return
Item names truncated to codes that mean nothing off the shelf
The return window is printed in the smallest type on the paper
rows.too_big_variant: A loyalty and returns system spanning app, email and paper.

rows.theme: Splitting one restaurant bill between four people who ordered differently.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: A familiar social problem where the awkwardness is the design problem, and students already know the failure cases.
pitfalls: Assumes an equal split, which is the one case that needs no design
Chasing the person who has not paid is left entirely undesigned
Turns into a payments product rather than one evening's arithmetic
rows.too_big_variant: A shared-expenses product covering rent, bills and holidays across months.

rows.theme: Setting up one regular payment to another person, and being sure it is right.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: Confirmation, review and error states carry the whole task, which is exactly what beginners skip.
pitfalls: The review step repeats the form instead of making the commitment legible
First payment date and frequency presented as unrelated fields
No state for 'set up but not yet sent', which is where users worry
rows.too_big_variant: A full payments area with international transfers, limits and beneficiaries.

rows.theme: A short check that tells someone whether it is worth applying for one benefit.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: The answer is often 'probably not', and designing an honest no is a genuinely hard first-year problem.
pitfalls: The 'no' result is designed as a dead end with nowhere to go
Asks fifteen questions when four would decide it
Students state eligibility rules as fact; the rules are the client's, not theirs
rows.too_big_variant: The full application, evidence upload and claim management journey.

rows.theme: Putting money aside for one named thing, and seeing whether it is on track.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: One number, one date, one progress state — a tight brief that rewards restraint and punishes decoration.
pitfalls: Progress shown only as a bar, with no sense of whether the pace is enough
Falling behind is styled as failure rather than as a decision point
Grows into budgeting, categories and charts nobody asked for
rows.too_big_variant: A personal finance manager with budgets, categories and spending analysis.

rows.theme: Showing a student that two of their classes clash, and what to do about it.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: Students are the users, so the research is free and the failures are ones they have personally suffered.
pitfalls: The clash is rendered as two overlapping blocks and never named as a problem
Week view designed first, so the one urgent conflict is buried in it
No route from noticing the clash to resolving it
rows.too_big_variant: A full timetabling system including room booking and staff availability.

rows.theme: The card on an exam desk carrying a candidate number and the rules that apply.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: Read once, under stress, at a fixed distance — a rare brief where the reading conditions are fully known.
pitfalls: The candidate number, the one thing that must be copied, is not the largest thing
Rules written for the invigilator rather than the candidate
Designed flat on screen, never checked lying at an angle on a desk

rows.theme: Returning written feedback on one piece of coursework so the student acts on it.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: Everyone in the room has received bad versions of this, so critique is grounded in experience rather than taste.
pitfalls: The mark is placed where it stops the feedback being read at all
Comments float free of the thing they refer to
'What to do next time' is designed as an afterthought, if at all
rows.too_big_variant: A submission and marking platform covering upload, plagiarism and moderation.

rows.theme: Reviewing one deck of thirty cards in five minutes on a bus.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: A single repeated interaction, so the portfolio has to be about rhythm and states rather than about screens.
pitfalls: The reveal and the self-rating are designed as one indistinct tap
No end state, so a five-minute session never feels finished
Becomes a deck-authoring tool instead of a review session
rows.too_big_variant: A study platform with deck sharing, scheduling algorithms and statistics.

rows.theme: A module reading list that shows what to read first and where to get it.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: Ordering and availability are the whole content, and both are usually thrown away in favour of a citation style.
pitfalls: Sorted alphabetically, which is the one order that helps nobody
Essential and optional given identical treatment
'Where to get it' reduced to a link that may or may not work
rows.too_big_variant: A library discovery system with search, holdings and reservations.

rows.theme: The notice on a lab door telling a first-time student what to do before entering.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: Read while walking, in seconds, and legally constrained — an unusually honest test of hierarchy.
pitfalls: Fifteen rules of equal weight, so the two that matter disappear
Hazard symbols used decoratively rather than as the entry point
Written for the person who already knows the lab
rows.too_big_variant: A departmental health and safety induction covering every room.

rows.theme: An enrolment form for a short evening course, filled in at a desk with a pen.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: Paper removes every interactive rescue, so field order, grouping and instructions have to do all the work.
pitfalls: Boxes sized for the designer's handwriting, not a real name or address
Instructions placed after the field they govern
Optional and required fields are indistinguishable once the pen is moving
rows.too_big_variant: An online admissions system with accounts, payments and document upload.

rows.theme: Scanning into a lecture in the thirty seconds before it starts.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: A hard time budget and a queue behind you, which makes every extra tap arguable in concrete terms.
pitfalls: Success and failure states look alike at a glance, so people scan twice
The failure case — no signal in the theatre — is never designed
Turns into an attendance analytics dashboard for staff
rows.too_big_variant: An engagement monitoring system with reports and interventions.

rows.theme: Offering one shift to colleagues and knowing when somebody has taken it.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: A two-sided task with a real handover moment, and the uncertainty in the middle is the design problem.
pitfalls: The offered-but-unclaimed state is not designed, so nobody knows where they stand
Assumes the swap is approved instantly when a manager is in the loop
Becomes a rota builder for the manager instead of the worker's task
rows.too_big_variant: A workforce management suite with rotas, payroll and compliance.

rows.theme: A weekly paper timesheet filled in by hand and signed by a supervisor.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: A grid with real arithmetic in it, and two readers with different needs sharing one sheet.
pitfalls: The total row is where the eye lands but the daily entries are what is checked
No room for the common case of a split shift
The signature block is placed as decoration rather than as the last action

rows.theme: Requesting three days off and seeing whether they have been approved.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: Waiting for someone else's decision is the core state, and beginners almost always design only the request.
pitfalls: Remaining allowance is shown after the dates are chosen, not before
Pending, approved and declined share one visual treatment
Partial approval — two of three days — has no design at all
rows.too_big_variant: An HR portal covering absence, sickness, appraisal and expenses.

rows.theme: The evacuation notice on the back of a door, read by someone who has never read it.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: A fixed size, a fixed position and a reader who is either bored or panicking — two very different design targets.
pitfalls: A plan drawn without a 'you are here' that matches where it hangs
Prose paragraphs where a numbered sequence is needed
Every notice in the building made identical, so orientation is lost
rows.too_big_variant: A building-wide emergency signage and drill programme.

rows.theme: Claiming back one train fare, with the receipt photographed on a phone.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: A short flow with a capture step, and the capture step is where it actually fails.
pitfalls: The photo is accepted without showing whether it is readable
Category fields written in finance's language rather than the claimant's
No state between submitted and paid, which is where the anxiety lives
rows.too_big_variant: A corporate travel and expense platform with policy, cards and approvals.

rows.theme: A handover note passed from one shift to the next in a care or retail setting.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: Written fast and read faster, by a colleague under time pressure — the constraint is honest and easy to test.
pitfalls: Free text only, so the urgent item hides in the middle of a paragraph
Every shift starts from blank, losing what was still outstanding
Designed for completeness when the reader has ninety seconds
rows.too_big_variant: An operations log covering incidents, staffing and stock across a region.

rows.theme: A job advert in a shop window, read from the pavement by a passer-by.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: Reading distance and glance time are fixed by the situation, which makes scale decisions checkable rather than arguable.
pitfalls: Pay and hours, the two things that decide it, are set smallest
Designed on a laptop and never printed and taped to a window
Becomes a poster about the business rather than an advert for the role

rows.theme: Signing in as a visitor at a reception desk and getting a badge that means something.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: A physical artefact produced by a short flow, and the badge has to be legible to a third person across a corridor.
pitfalls: The badge shows the visitor's name large and the host's name not at all
Previous visitors' details left visible on a shared sheet or screen
The sign-out step, which is the one that matters in a fire, is undesigned
rows.too_big_variant: A building access system with passes, contractors and permissions.

rows.theme: The label beside one museum object, read by a visitor who is already tired.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: Forty words, a fixed rectangle, and a reader standing up — a brief so tight that every cut has to be justified.
pitfalls: Curatorial voice kept intact, so the label is written for other curators
Accession numbers given the same weight as the thing the visitor wants to know
Designed on screen and never checked at the height it will hang
rows.too_big_variant: An interpretation scheme for a whole gallery, with themes and trails.

rows.theme: A ticket that gets one person into a venue and to the right part of it.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: Scanned by staff and read by the holder, often on a dim phone screen — two readers, one small surface.
pitfalls: Door time and start time not distinguished, which is the most common real failure
Barcode placed where a thumb naturally sits
Designed only as a screen, never as the printed version some people still bring
rows.too_big_variant: A ticketing platform with seating plans, resale and box office tools.

rows.theme: Handing one playlist to a friend so they can actually listen to it.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: One feature rather than one product, which is the difference between a markable portfolio and a redesign.
pitfalls: Expands into a whole listening product within a week
The state where the friend has no account is skipped entirely
Sharing designed without designing what the receiver sees first
rows.too_big_variant: A streaming service with library, discovery, social and playback.

rows.theme: The shelf-end guide that tells a library visitor what is in this run of shelving.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: A classification the student did not invent, presented to someone who does not know it exists.
pitfalls: Reproduces the classification codes without translating them
Set for the person walking towards it rather than standing at it
Every shelf end made identical, so they stop being navigational

rows.theme: What is on at one cinema today, for someone deciding in the next ten minutes.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: A tight time frame turns an ordinary listing into a real prioritisation problem with a testable answer.
pitfalls: Shows the whole week when the question was about tonight
Screenings that have already started are listed as if bookable
Poster images crowd out the times, which are the actual content
rows.too_big_variant: A chain-wide booking site with memberships, seat selection and food ordering.

rows.theme: A weekly schedule for a small community radio station, for a listener with one favourite show.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: A grid with genuinely irregular content, which breaks the tidy tables students default to.
pitfalls: A seven-column grid that collapses into unreadable columns on a phone
Repeats and first broadcasts given identical treatment
'On air now' is designed as an afterthought rather than the entry point
rows.too_big_variant: A station site with on-demand archives, podcasts and presenter pages.

rows.theme: The printed floor plan handed to a visitor at the door of an exhibition.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: Held, folded and carried around while walking, so orientation and folding are part of the design, not after it.
pitfalls: Drawn to architectural convention rather than to the route people walk
No orientation cue, so the plan is useless once the visitor turns around
Room numbers used that do not appear anywhere on the walls
rows.too_big_variant: A museum-wide visitor guide covering every floor and facility.

rows.theme: Six people choosing the next book, and everyone knowing what was chosen.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: A small group decision with a clear ending, so the portfolio must design agreement rather than just a vote.
pitfalls: Designed as a poll and never as a decision that has to be announced
No state for 'still deciding', which is where the group actually lives
Turns into a reading social network with reviews and profiles
rows.too_big_variant: A reading community platform with reviews, shelves and recommendations.

rows.theme: The timetable panel at one bus stop, read in the rain by someone in a hurry.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: Fixed size, fixed height, unforgiving conditions, and a reader with exactly one question.
pitfalls: Full-week timetable given where 'the next one is at 14:12' is the question
Route numbers set smaller than the operator's branding
Set in a size that works on screen and not at a metre in poor light
rows.too_big_variant: A network-wide passenger information system across stops and apps.

rows.theme: Buying one single fare from a machine while a queue forms behind you.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: Standing, hurried, watched, one finger — constraints students can experience directly and cheaply.
pitfalls: Fare options presented as a full tariff rather than the two people actually buy
Card, receipt and ticket returned in an order nobody decided
Touch targets sized for a phone rather than a gloved hand at a panel
rows.too_big_variant: A full retail estate covering season tickets, refunds and railcards.

rows.theme: The next three departures from one stop, for a person already walking towards it.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: A single glanceable answer where every added feature measurably costs the reader time.
pitfalls: Delays shown as a status word with no revised time attached
Cancelled services removed silently instead of being shown as cancelled
Becomes a journey planner rather than an answer to one question
rows.too_big_variant: A journey planning product with routing, tickets and disruption alerts.

rows.theme: A printed notice at a station explaining that one line is closed this weekend.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: Bad news plus an alternative, on paper, for people who are already moving — a genuinely hard hierarchy problem.
pitfalls: The dates of the closure are less prominent than the apology
The replacement route is described in words with no map or stop names
One notice designed for a network of stations with different alternatives

rows.theme: Unlocking one hire bike from a stand, and knowing the hire has actually started.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: A physical outcome the screen only reports on, which forces students to design feedback rather than buttons.
pitfalls: Confirmation shown before the lock has actually released
No design for the bike that will not unlock, which is the common case
Turns into a membership and pricing product instead of one unlock
rows.too_big_variant: A bike share service covering accounts, pricing, maps and faults.

rows.theme: A residents' parking permit application, filled in with documents on the table.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: Evidence requirements drive the structure, and getting them in the wrong order visibly wastes the applicant's time.
pitfalls: Document requirements revealed at the end rather than the start
Vehicle and address treated as one section when they have different sources
The renewal case, which is most applicants, is not designed
rows.too_big_variant: A parking services portal with fines, appeals and visitor permits.

rows.theme: Claiming a refund for one delayed journey, using a ticket you may have thrown away.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: The evidence problem is real and the flow has an outcome — a rare student brief with a genuine ending.
pitfalls: Assumes the ticket still exists and offers no path when it does not
Eligibility rules restated in operator language rather than plainly
No state between claimed and paid, which can be six weeks
rows.too_big_variant: A customer relations system covering complaints, compensation and correspondence.

rows.theme: The platform and exit signs at a small station, for a passenger changing trains.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: Decision points are few and physical, so the student can walk the route and count the failures.
pitfalls: Signs visible only once the passenger has already chosen a direction
Exit and interchange information competing at the same size
Designed as one sign rather than as the sequence a passenger passes
rows.too_big_variant: A national station signage standard.

rows.theme: The allergen card handed over in a cafe when someone asks what is safe to eat.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: A grid with a real consequence, handled quickly at a counter, where ambiguity is not merely untidy.
pitfalls: A tick grid so dense it cannot be read standing at a till
'May contain' and 'contains' rendered identically
Designed for the fourteen allergens rather than the one this customer has

rows.theme: Knowing where one takeaway order has got to, without ringing the shop.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: Waiting is the entire experience, so the portfolio must be about states over time rather than about screens.
pitfalls: A progress bar that moves on a timer rather than on real events
No design for 'later than promised', which is when the screen is actually opened
Becomes a food ordering marketplace instead of one order's status
rows.too_big_variant: A delivery marketplace with restaurants, checkout, tracking and ratings.

rows.theme: Cooking one recipe from a screen with wet hands and a pan already hot.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: The physical context rules out most interaction ideas immediately, which is a useful discipline early on.
pitfalls: Ingredients and steps on separate screens, so the cook keeps going back
Text sized for reading in the hand, not on a worktop at arm's length
Timings buried in prose rather than pulled out where they can be acted on
rows.too_big_variant: A recipe platform with search, meal plans, shopping lists and video.

rows.theme: The price sign on one market stall, read across two metres of produce.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: Handwritten conventions the student must study rather than invent, and a distance that settles the type size argument.
pitfalls: Unit and price given equal weight, so 'per kilo' is missed
Offers designed so the original price is more prominent than the new one
Designed as one sign rather than a stall's worth seen together

rows.theme: A referral form that gets one household a food parcel this week.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: Dignity is a design variable here, and it can be argued about concretely rather than abstractly.
pitfalls: Asks for justification before it asks what is needed
Household composition captured in a way that cannot express real households
Designed for the charity's reporting rather than for the referral
rows.too_big_variant: A case management system for a network of distribution centres.

rows.theme: A shopping list two people add to separately and one of them takes to the shop.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: Two users, one artefact, and a moment of use in an aisle — the conflict is built into the brief.
pitfalls: Ordered by when items were added rather than how the shop is walked
No visible sign that the other person has changed something
Turns into a household organiser with chores, budgets and calendars
rows.too_big_variant: A household management product covering tasks, meals and budgets.

rows.theme: A canteen receipt that also has to carry nutrition information someone might use.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: Two purposes on one narrow strip of paper, and the second purpose is usually sacrificed without a decision.
pitfalls: Nutrition data added at the bottom in the smallest type available
Per-item and per-meal figures not distinguished
Designed as a data dump rather than for the one figure a reader wants

rows.theme: Knowing what in the fridge needs eating tonight before it is thrown away.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: Entry cost is the whole problem — anything that takes effort to record will not be recorded.
pitfalls: Requires typing every item in, so it is abandoned after two shops
Sorted by date added rather than by what expires first
Grows into inventory management for a whole kitchen
rows.too_big_variant: A kitchen inventory product with barcodes, recipes and waste reporting.

rows.theme: An energy bill that shows what was used, what it cost, and what changed.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: Real numbers, a comparison over time, and a reader who is often anxious — hierarchy with a genuine stake.
pitfalls: The amount due is designed and the reason for the change is not
Estimated and actual readings shown without distinguishing them
Comparison charts added decoratively with no baseline stated
rows.too_big_variant: An energy account area with tariffs, meters, payments and switching.

rows.theme: Submitting one meter reading, from a cupboard, with a torch.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: The capture conditions are terrible and knowable, so the design must answer them rather than assume a desk.
pitfalls: No guidance on which digits to read, which is the actual failure
A validation error phrased as a rejection rather than a question
The confirmation does not show what was submitted, so it cannot be checked
rows.too_big_variant: A smart metering product with usage analysis and tariff advice.

rows.theme: The letter telling a tenant how much of their deposit is being returned, and why.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: Money, disagreement and a deadline to challenge — the design decides whether the challenge route is findable.
pitfalls: Deductions listed without saying what evidence supports each one
The dispute deadline is present but not treated as the urgent element
Students write the landlord's justification, which is not theirs to write

rows.theme: Reporting a broken boiler to a landlord and getting an appointment out of it.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: Urgency has to be communicated by the tenant and understood by the landlord — two readings of the same input.
pitfalls: Urgency captured as a dropdown nobody can calibrate
Photographs requested with no guidance, so they show nothing useful
The flow ends at 'reported' with no appointment and no expectation set
rows.too_big_variant: A property management system covering tenancies, contractors and compliance.

rows.theme: The control panel on a washing machine, used by someone who did not buy it.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: A fixed physical layout with no undo and no help text, so labelling and mapping carry the entire load.
pitfalls: Symbols reproduced from the manual without checking anyone reads them
Programme names that describe the machine's behaviour, not the clothes
The two settings people change are given the same treatment as sixteen they never touch
rows.too_big_variant: A connected appliance ecosystem with an app, profiles and diagnostics.

rows.theme: The first-week checklist for someone who has just moved into a rented flat.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: Sequence and dependency are the content, and students can test it against their own move.
pitfalls: A flat list where half the items depend on another being done first
No sense of which items have a deadline attached
Becomes a moving-house product with quotes, inventories and suppliers
rows.too_big_variant: A relocation service covering removals, utilities and paperwork.

rows.theme: The card left behind after a smoke alarm test, telling a resident what was found.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: Left on a table and read hours later by someone who was not there — the artefact has to explain itself completely.
pitfalls: Says the test was done but not whether anything needs doing
Engineer's shorthand reproduced for a reader who cannot decode it
The action required is placed below the signature block

rows.theme: The card put through the door when a parcel could not be delivered.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: One small card carrying a choice, a location and a deadline — every hierarchy mistake shows up immediately.
pitfalls: The deadline for collection is the least prominent thing on the card
Options presented as equal when one is far more likely
Reference numbers printed too small to copy accurately
rows.too_big_variant: A parcel tracking and redelivery service across web, app and messaging.

rows.theme: A poster for one event, on a crowded noticeboard, competing with thirty others.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: Competition for attention is literal and testable — pin the mock-up up and see whether it wins.
pitfalls: Designed in isolation and never seen against other posters
The date and place lose out to an illustration
Tear-off strips added without deciding what should be on them
rows.too_big_variant: A campaign identity across print, social and local press.

rows.theme: A lost pet notice on a lamp post, read by someone walking past at speed.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: Emotional content with a strictly practical job, and weather and distance both constrain the result.
pitfalls: The photograph is chosen for sentiment rather than for identification
The contact number is set smaller than the word LOST
Ignores rain, tape and the fact it will be read from two metres away

rows.theme: Signing up for one volunteering shift at a community kitchen next Saturday.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: A commitment made in a moment and honoured a week later, so reminders and cancellation are part of the design.
pitfalls: What the shift actually involves is not shown before the commitment
No dignified way to withdraw, so people simply do not turn up
Becomes a volunteer management system for the coordinator
rows.too_big_variant: A volunteering platform with roles, rotas, checks and reporting.

rows.theme: Borrowing one drill from a tool library and knowing when it is due back.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: A physical object, a due date and a shared resource — scarcity makes the states meaningful rather than decorative.
pitfalls: Availability shown without saying when an item comes back
The due date is designed once and never surfaced again before it passes
Turns into a catalogue product rather than one borrow and return
rows.too_big_variant: A library management system with members, fines, stock and reservations.

rows.theme: The council form for closing one residential street for an afternoon.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: An unfamiliar bureaucratic task with a friendly purpose, where plain language does visible work.
pitfalls: Notice periods stated in the middle of the form rather than at the start
Neighbour consent handled as a tick rather than as the task it is
Written in highways language throughout because the source was
rows.too_big_variant: An events licensing portal covering road closures, alcohol and safety.

rows.theme: A weekly summary of what a busy neighbourhood group has been discussing.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: Summarising and ranking other people's content forces editorial decisions students must then defend.
pitfalls: Everything included, which reproduces the problem the digest exists to solve
Ordered by activity, so the loudest thread always leads
Things needing a response are not separated from things to read
rows.too_big_variant: A neighbourhood social network with groups, marketplace and messaging.

rows.theme: Asking neighbours for one specific piece of help, without having to explain yourself.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: The hardest part is asking, so the design problem is emotional and structural at once — and it is nameable.
pitfalls: Requires a public profile before a request can be made
Requests and offers presented in one undifferentiated stream
No design for the request that has been answered, so it stays up
rows.too_big_variant: A mutual aid platform covering areas, verification and coordination.

rows.theme: Booking one community hall for two hours on a Tuesday evening.
rows.why_it_works_at_L4: Availability, price and rules are all real constraints, and the booking has an unambiguous confirmation.
pitfalls: Availability shown as a month grid when the question is one evening
Deposit and key collection, which decide the booking, are mentioned last
The recurring booking case is designed before the single one works
rows.too_big_variant: A venue management system with invoicing, keyholders and maintenance.

known_gaps: No domain fell short of five; all ten hold eight. That is a product of authoring rather than of collection, and it should be read as an even spread rather than as evidence that eight was the right number for each.

Forty-three of the eighty are not products, well above the fifteen rule 4 asks for. This was deliberate — the module is called Screen Design and the non-product themes are the ones that force a student to argue about hierarchy without a component library to hide in — but a tutor who wants the bank weighted the other way should cut from here rather than add apps.

Every theme assumes a UK-shaped institution (a council, a tenancy deposit, a residents' permit). None require a non-Latin script or a right-to-left reading order, so the bank cannot on its own produce a portfolio that tests those.
screen_count_estimate is an author's judgement, not an observation. It has not been checked against a completed Level 4 portfolio, and the first cohort is the thing that will correct it.

screen_count_estimate never goes above six, so the 7-9 band the schema allows is unused. The bank therefore has nothing to offer a student who wants more scope, and a tutor asking for a larger theme has to build it rather than pick it.
No theme was tested with a student. The claim in why_it_works_at_L4 is a teaching hypothesis in every row.
notes.method: Authored, not collected — there is no external source for a teaching construct, so nothing here is sourced and nothing here claims to be. Written domain by domain to eight each, then read back against the brief's test: could two students given this theme produce visibly different portfolios, and would either be markable against the three learning outcomes. Themes that survived only as categories ('a booking app for X') were cut rather than narrowed. Brand names were avoided in themes and in pitfalls alike, per rule 5. example_screen_ids is null on every row and was never populated, per rule 3. The eighty is the ceiling in the schema, not a target that was worked towards.
